activities.caption: rebuild the spike — phase by phase
activities.name: nePhaseOrder

config.prompt: One action potential, left to right across the curve. Rebuild the phases:
items: Resting — about −70 mV, maintained by the sodium–potassium pump
Hyperpolarisation — a brief dip below rest
Recovery — the original ion distribution restored
config.why: The spike is all-or-nothing: stronger stimuli do not produce bigger spikes, only more frequent ones — information rides in firing frequency.

activities.anchor: the same cell type can serve seeing, moving and remembering
activities.caption: pair each part with its job
activities.name: nePartsMatch

config.prompt: One design, local specialisations. Pair each component with its job:

pairs.right: branching antennae collecting signals from hundreds to thousands of neurons
sums excitation against inhibition every millisecond
output cable — in humans sometimes a metre long, only micrometres across
where the spike is converted into a chemical message
the immune cells of the supporting cast

config.why: Glia outnumber neurons roughly one to one, and interneurons are the overwhelming majority — the brain is mostly processing, not wiring to the periphery.

activities.anchor: does not wash through the brain
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a pop-science script
activities.name: neChemSpot

config.prompt: A popular-science script about brain chemistry contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: 'Serotonin is the brain's chemical for happiness — released, it bathes the brain in good mood.'
A transmitter acts on the few receptors within nanometres of its release site.
It is then pumped back or destroyed within milliseconds.
Chemicals act locally at specific synapses, like transistors with chemistry.
config.correction: There are no chemicals for emotions: the brain is a circuit of spiking cells, and a transmitter released at one connection acts only locally — it never bathes the brain.
config.why: The neuron is an electrical device made of salt water, protein and a membrane; its chemistry is point-to-point, at specific synapses.

activities.anchor: so sodium is kept scarce inside
activities.caption: call the gradient — the pump's work
activities.name: neGradientEstimate

config.prompt: The sodium–potassium pump burns ATP to hold the gradients. Roughly how many times more potassium does the cell keep inside than outside?
config.why: Roughly 20–40× more K⁺ inside than outside — a battery built from salt, charged by exporting 3 Na⁺ for every 2 K⁺ imported.
config.context: At equilibrium the potassium Nernst potential is about −90 mV; rest sits near −70 mV because a little sodium also leaks in.

activities.anchor: closed at rest but snap open
activities.caption: place the marker — the trigger point
activities.name: neThresholdPlace

config.prompt: Voltage-gated sodium channels snap open past a trigger voltage. Place the marker at threshold:
config.why: Threshold sits near −55 mV: subthreshold inputs die out, and past it the full spike fires — binary, noise-resistant signalling like computer logic.

activities.caption: true or false — the pump and the spike
activities.name: nePumpJudge

statements.s: The sodium–potassium pump fires the spike, spending ATP on each action potential as it happens.
statements.why: The spike is passive chemistry: channels open and ions run down gradients the pump built earlier.

statements.s: The pump restores concentrations over thousands of spikes.
statements.why: Slow bookkeeping — which is why a poison blocking the pump silences a neuron only after a delay.

statements.s: Tetrodotoxin, of pufferfish fame, silences a neuron instantly.
statements.why: It blocks the channels themselves, so no spike can regenerate at all.

statements.s: Blocking the pump and blocking the channels silence a neuron on the same timescale.
statements.why: Channel block is instant; pump block waits for the stored gradients to run down.
